initial_request.raw_prompt: Modernize the existing e-commerce monolith for incremental evolution and improved scalability. The system must support up to 50,000 concurrent users during peak campaigns, remain highly available and responsive, run on AWS, comply with GDPR, and remain operational during the migration. No fixed monetary budget has been defined; cost efficiency should be considered.

behavior.overview: This repository is an e-commerce web application structured as a Django-based backend API with a React-based frontend. It supports full product catalog management, user authentication, customer profile management, address handling, order processing, secure payments, and customer reviews.

partitions.name: Backend API (Django)
partitions.role: Serves as the server-side REST API, handling business logic, database migrations, and data models for all e-commerce domains.
partitions.functionality: Provides CRUD operations for products, orders, user accounts, and reviews while managing payment status, shipping addresses, and geo-data (countries/states/cities).

partitions.name: Frontend Application (React)
partitions.role: The client-side user interface that consumes the Django API to provide a shopping experience.
partitions.functionality: Includes product displays, cart management, user authentication forms, order tracking, and state management using Redux to handle shopping sessions and data updates.

partitions.name: Static Assets
partitions.role: Provides production-ready assets for the Django admin dashboard and the integrated frontend build.
partitions.functionality: Contains compiled CSS, JavaScript chunks, fonts, and images required for the admin interface and the React SPA deployment.

context_record.business_goal: Modernize the existing e-commerce monolith so it can scale during peak traffic, remain maintainable as the business grows, and evolve incrementally without disrupting ongoing operations.
context_record.problem_statement: The current monolith has scalability and maintainability problems, especially during peak traffic. Changes are difficult to deploy safely, and tightly coupled functionality makes independent evolution difficult.

blueprint.rationale: The Strangler Fig pattern enables incremental extraction of capabilities from the existing Django monolith into independent services while preserving continuous operation. This aligns with the business goal of scaling during peak traffic, improving maintainability, and supporting zero‑downtime evolution on AWS.
blueprint.stakeholder_view: Online customers interact with a responsive React SPA that communicates via a unified API Gateway. Customer support, warehouse staff, finance, and product management gain faster feature delivery because each business capability (user accounts, catalog, orders, payments, reviews) is owned by a dedicated service that can be scaled, updated, and deployed independently. Operations staff benefit from automated scaling, health‑checks, and clear ownership of services, reducing operational risk during traffic spikes.
blueprint.technical_view: An AWS API Gateway fronts the system, routing HTTP requests to either the Legacy Monolith (for not‑yet‑extracted functionality) or to newly created domain services (User, Product, Order, Payment, Review). Each service is a Python/Django application with its own schema in a shared PostgreSQL cluster, ensuring data ownership. Internal communication uses a hybrid model: synchronous HTTP for UI‑driven calls and asynchronous events via Amazon SNS/SQS for cross‑service workflows (e.g., order creation, payment processing). Services are deployed in ECS/Fargate with auto‑scaling groups across multiple AZs, backed by an RDS PostgreSQL instance and managed queues. Feature flags in the gateway enable gradual traffic shift during migration steps.

adrs.title: ADR-001: Service decomposition using Domain-Driven Design
adrs.context: The monolith tightly couples user, product, order, payment, and review capabilities, hindering independent scaling and evolution.
adrs.decision: Define bounded contexts aligned with business capabilities and implement each as an independent Django service.
adrs.rationale: DDD aligns service boundaries with natural domain divisions, reducing coupling and enabling independent deployment, which directly addresses scalability and maintainability goals.
negative_consequences: Need for data synchronization during migration

adrs.title: ADR-002: Service-specific data ownership
adrs.context: Shared database tables across domains cause tight coupling and hinder independent evolution.
adrs.decision: Each service owns its own schema within a shared PostgreSQL cluster; no service accesses another's tables directly.
adrs.rationale: Service‑owned data enforces boundaries, simplifies migrations, and supports independent scaling, matching the DDD approach.
alternatives_considered: Single shared schema for all services

adrs.title: ADR-003: Hybrid integration (sync UI, async events)
adrs.context: User‑facing interactions require low‑latency responses, while internal workflows benefit from decoupling.
adrs.decision: Use synchronous HTTP for UI‑driven calls via API Gateway and asynchronous event‑driven communication (SNS/SQS) for inter‑service processes.
adrs.rationale: Combines responsive user experience with scalable, fault‑tolerant backend processing, as recommended for e‑commerce workloads.
positive_consequences: Loose coupling and better fault isolation
negative_consequences: Added complexity of managing queues and eventual consistency

adrs.title: ADR-004: AWS auto-scaling and multi-AZ deployment
adrs.context: Peak traffic of up to 50,000 concurrent users requires elastic capacity and high availability.
adrs.decision: Deploy services in AWS ECS/Fargate with auto‑scaling groups and place them behind an Application Load Balancer across multiple Availability Zones. Use RDS Multi‑AZ for PostgreSQL.
adrs.rationale: AWS managed scaling and multi‑AZ provide the elasticity and resilience needed without manual capacity planning, directly supporting the required scalability and availability targets.
negative_consequences: Potential cost increase if scaling is not tuned

adrs.title: ADR-005: Incremental migration via Strangler Fig
adrs.context: The need to modernize without disrupting ongoing operations.
adrs.decision: Introduce a façade (API Gateway) and migrate capabilities one bounded context at a time, routing traffic via feature flags until the monolith can be retired.
adrs.rationale: Strangler Fig enables zero‑downtime migration, aligns with the incremental migration requirement, and leverages existing AWS routing capabilities.
negative_consequences: Complexity of dual‑write and routing logic

adrs.title: ADR-006: Preserve existing Python/Django and React stack
adrs.context: The repository already uses Python/Django for backend and React for frontend; no compelling requirement to replace them.
adrs.decision: Retain Python/Django for all new services and keep the React SPA unchanged, adding only AWS managed infrastructure where needed.
adrs.rationale: Reusing the existing stack minimizes rewrite effort, leverages team expertise, and reduces risk, while still achieving scalability via cloud services.
alternatives_considered: Rewrite services in a different language/framework
positive_consequences: Faster migration due to familiar codebase
negative_consequences: Potential limitations of Django for certain high‑throughput scenarios

retrieved_knowledge.content:
The reviewed studies reveal several distinct approaches to monolith decomposition, each with specific advantages for e-commerce contexts.

**a. Domain-Driven Design (DDD) Approaches:** Multiple studies emphasize Domain-Driven Design as a foundational approach for identifying service boundaries in e-commerce systems. Abgaz et al. [1] identify DDD as a critical component of their Monolith to Microservices Decomposition Framework (M2MDF), noting its effectiveness in creating business-aligned service boundaries. Kaloudis [6] reinforces this approach, demonstrating how DDD enables better service cohesion and reduced coupling. In e-commerce contexts, natural domain boundaries often align with business capabilities, such as customer management, product catalog, order processing, payment handling, and inventory management.

Microservices architecture has emerged as a compelling alternative, offering the promise of enhanced scalability, improved fault tolerance, and greater development agility [1]. By decomposing monolithic applications into smaller, independently deployable services, organizations can achieve better resource utilization, faster deployment cycles, and improved system resilience.

Event-driven architecture (EDA) patterns have gained particular attention in the context of microservices migration, especially for e-commerce systems where business processes are inherently event-oriented. Customer actions such as placing orders, updating profiles, or processing payments naturally translate to domain events that can drive system behavior [5]. The asynchronous nature of event-driven communication provides better decoupling between services, enhanced fault tolerance, and improved scalability compared to synchronous request-response patterns [4].

**Solution mechanics:** Each service exclusively owns its data; persistent data is accessed only through that service's API, never by another service reaching into its tables. Implementation variants (increasing isolation): private-tables-per-service, schema-per-service, and database-server-per-service (private-tables and schema-per-service have the lowest overhead). True database-per-service means separate connection strings, credentials, and lifecycle management, so a team can migrate or upgrade its database without coordinating with others. Because a single ACID transaction can no longer span services, cross-service data operations are implemented as a series of local transactions coordinated by **Sagas**, and cross-service queries use **API Composition** (the caller/gateway joins results from multiple services) or **CQRS materialized views** (a view subscribes to services' events). The **Transactional Outbox** pattern atomically updates a service's database and publishes an event.

**b. High Load Scenarios:** Asynchronous patterns (message queues) demonstrate superior throughput and availability [4].

**c. Availability:** Event-driven architectures provide better fault tolerance and system availability under stress [4].

These findings suggest that e-commerce systems should employ hybrid approaches, using synchronous communication for real-time user interactions and asynchronous patterns for backend processing and inter-service communication.

## 2.2 Monolithic and Microservices Architectures Comparison *(printed p. 478)*

In the e-commerce landscape, choosing between microservices and traditional monolithic architectures requires careful consideration of various factors. Monolithic architectures, characterized by their single, tightly coupled codebase. However, when e-commerce systems increase in size, they frequently face scalability and maintenance issues. Microservices provide an alternative approach by decomposing monolithic applications into smaller, self-contained services [6]. This decomposition results in fine-grained services, each focusing on a specific business capability. Scalability is one of the most major advantages of microservices. E-commerce platforms often experience fluctuating traffic patterns, especially during promotions or seasonal events. Microservices enable organisations to scale individual services, ensuring that resources are deployed efficiently to manage workload properly.

# Monolith-to-Microservices-Migration im E-Commerce: Zerlegung, Event-Driven Patterns und Leistung (kuratorischer Auszug)

- **Source title:** Migrating Monolithic E-Commerce Systems to Microservices: A Systematic Review of Event-Driven Architecture Approaches (curated excerpts)
- **Author(s):** Stephen W. Bulus, Olubukola D. Adekola, Folasade Y. Ayankoya, Oluwabamise J. Adeniyi, Ayodeji G. Abiodun
- **Year:** 2025
- **Knowledge box:** 2
- **Domain:** e-commerce
- **Original PDF:** `AJSTE_O1G0V4GO.pdf`

## Introduction — relevante Absätze zur E-Commerce-Migration *(printed p. 2)*

The rapid evolution of e-commerce platforms has necessitated architectural paradigm shifts to meet increasing demands for scalability, reliability, and agility [2]. Traditional monolithic architectures, while providing simplicity in development and deployment, often become bottlenecks as e-commerce systems scale to handle millions of transactions and users [3]. The centralized nature of monolithic systems creates inherent limitations in terms of independent scaling, technology diversity, and fault isolation, making them unsuitable for modern e-commerce requirements.

With a domain-driven microservices approach, each service uses the database that fits its data characteristics. Each microservice owns its private data store. This design prevents unintentional coupling between services and supports independent updates and deployments without coordinating changes across the system.

features.name: User Account Management
features.description: Enable customers to create, authenticate, and manage their personal accounts.
features.scenario: A new customer registers, verifies their email, logs in, updates their profile information, and logs out successfully.
acceptance_criteria: Registration completes and a verification email is sent.
Login succeeds with the registered credentials.
Profile updates are persisted and reflected on subsequent logins.
Password reset flow works and allows the user to set a new password.

features.name: Product Browsing and Management
features.description: Provide customers with searchable product listings and allow staff to maintain the catalog.
features.scenario: A customer searches for a product category, applies filters, views product details, and an admin adds a new product that becomes immediately searchable.
acceptance_criteria: Search returns relevant products matching keywords and filters.
Product detail page loads with correct information and images.
Newly added product appears in search results within a short period.
Updates to product information are reflected in subsequent queries.

features.name: Order Processing
features.description: Allow customers to place orders and track their status through the fulfillment workflow.
features.scenario: A logged‑in customer adds items to the cart, proceeds to checkout, confirms the order, and receives an order confirmation with a status that updates as the order is processed.
acceptance_criteria: Order is created and a unique order ID is generated.
Inventory is reserved for the ordered items.
Customer receives an order confirmation email containing the order ID.
Order status transitions (e.g., confirmed, packed, shipped) are visible to the customer.

features.name: Payment Integration
features.description: Integrate with external payment gateways to capture funds securely.
features.scenario: During checkout, the customer selects a payment method, the system forwards the transaction to the payment provider, and handles both successful and declined responses.
acceptance_criteria: Successful payment results in order status 'paid' and a receipt email.
Declined payment returns a clear error message and does not create a paid order.
Payment transaction details are stored for reconciliation.
PCI‑DSS relevant data is never stored in the application database.

features.name: Product Review Functionality
features.description: Enable customers to submit and view reviews for purchased products.
features.scenario: A verified purchaser writes a review with a rating and comment; after moderation, the review appears on the product page.
acceptance_criteria: Only customers with a completed purchase can submit a review.
Submitted review is stored and flagged for moderation.
Approved reviews are displayed on the product detail page.
Review rating contributes to the product's average rating.

features.name: Scalability for Peak Traffic
features.description: Ensure the system can handle the expected peak load of 50,000 concurrent users.
features.scenario: During a simulated marketing campaign, 50,000 concurrent virtual users perform typical browsing and checkout actions without error or degradation.
acceptance_criteria: The system processes all requests without HTTP 5xx errors.
Response times remain within acceptable user‑experience limits (no noticeable slowdown).
Resource utilization stays within the capacity of provisioned AWS services.

features.name: High Availability
features.description: Maintain service continuity during component failures or infrastructure incidents.
features.scenario: A primary application instance is terminated; traffic is automatically rerouted to healthy instances with no interruption to active user sessions.
acceptance_criteria: No user‑visible downtime is observed during the failover event.
In‑flight requests are completed successfully or retried transparently.
Health checks detect the failure and trigger automatic recovery within a short period.

features.name: Responsive Customer‑Facing Interactions
features.description: Provide fast, interactive experiences for end‑users across all front‑end operations.
features.scenario: A customer performs a product search, views a product page, adds an item to the cart, and proceeds to checkout, each step completing without perceptible lag.
acceptance_criteria: UI actions (search, navigation, add‑to‑cart) complete within a responsive time perceived as instantaneous by users.
No UI freezes or long loading indicators appear under normal load.
Performance remains consistent across browsers and device types.

features.name: Elastic Scaling
features.description: Automatically adjust compute resources in response to changing demand.
features.scenario: As traffic gradually rises from baseline to peak, the platform adds additional compute capacity; when traffic falls, excess capacity is released, all without manual intervention.
acceptance_criteria: Scaling events are triggered by defined metrics (e.g., CPU, request rate).
New capacity becomes available within a short time after scaling out.
Scaling in reduces resource usage without impacting active sessions.

features.name: Incremental Migration Support

Inventory is reserved for the ordered items.
Customer receives an order confirmation email containing the order ID.
Order status transitions (e.g., confirmed, packed, shipped) are visible to the customer.

features.name: Payment Integration
features.description: Integrate with external payment gateways to capture funds securely.
features.scenario: During checkout, the customer selects a payment method, the system forwards the transaction to the payment provider, and handles both successful and declined responses.
acceptance_criteria: Successful payment results in order status 'paid' and a receipt email.
Declined payment returns a clear error message and does not create a paid order.
Payment transaction details are stored for reconciliation.
PCI‑DSS relevant data is never stored in the application database.

features.name: Product Review Functionality
features.description: Enable customers to submit and view reviews for purchased products.
features.scenario: A verified purchaser writes a review with a rating and comment; after moderation, the review appears on the product page.
acceptance_criteria: Only customers with a completed purchase can submit a review.
Submitted review is stored and flagged for moderation.
Approved reviews are displayed on the product detail page.
Review rating contributes to the product's average rating.

features.name: Scalability for Peak Traffic
features.description: Ensure the system can handle the expected peak load of 50,000 concurrent users.
features.scenario: During a simulated marketing campaign, 50,000 concurrent virtual users perform typical browsing and checkout actions without error or degradation.
acceptance_criteria: The system processes all requests without HTTP 5xx errors.
Response times remain within acceptable user‑experience limits (no noticeable slowdown).
Resource utilization stays within the capacity of provisioned AWS services.

features.name: High Availability
features.description: Maintain service continuity during component failures or infrastructure incidents.
features.scenario: A primary application instance is terminated; traffic is automatically rerouted to healthy instances with no interruption to active user sessions.
acceptance_criteria: No user‑visible downtime is observed during the failover event.
In‑flight requests are completed successfully or retried transparently.
Health checks detect the failure and trigger automatic recovery within a short period.

features.name: Responsive Customer‑Facing Interactions
features.description: Provide fast, interactive experiences for end‑users across all front‑end operations.
features.scenario: A customer performs a product search, views a product page, adds an item to the cart, and proceeds to checkout, each step completing without perceptible lag.
acceptance_criteria: UI actions (search, navigation, add‑to‑cart) complete within a responsive time perceived as instantaneous by users.
No UI freezes or long loading indicators appear under normal load.
Performance remains consistent across browsers and device types.

features.name: Elastic Scaling
features.description: Automatically adjust compute resources in response to changing demand.
features.scenario: As traffic gradually rises from baseline to peak, the platform adds additional compute capacity; when traffic falls, excess capacity is released, all without manual intervention.
acceptance_criteria: Scaling events are triggered by defined metrics (e.g., CPU, request rate).
New capacity becomes available within a short time after scaling out.
Scaling in reduces resource usage without impacting active sessions.

features.name: Incremental Migration Support
features.description: Allow new services to be introduced and traffic shifted gradually without disrupting existing operations.
features.scenario: A new microservice handling product catalog queries is deployed alongside the monolith; a portion of traffic is routed to the microservice using feature flags, and the switch is completed with zero downtime.
acceptance_criteria: Both the monolith and the new service can run concurrently.
Traffic can be shifted incrementally via routing rules or feature flags.
If a rollback is required, traffic can be returned to the monolith without service interruption.

blueprint.rationale: The Strangler Fig pattern enables incremental extraction of capabilities from the existing Django monolith into independent services while preserving continuous operation. This aligns with the business goal of scaling during peak traffic, improving maintainability, and supporting zero‑downtime evolution on AWS.
blueprint.stakeholder_view: Online customers interact with a responsive React SPA that communicates via a unified API Gateway. Customer support, warehouse staff, finance, and product management gain faster feature delivery because each business capability (user accounts, catalog, orders, payments, reviews) is owned by a dedicated service that can be scaled, updated, and deployed independently. Operations staff benefit from automated scaling, health‑checks, and clear ownership of services, reducing operational risk during traffic spikes.
blueprint.technical_view: An AWS API Gateway fronts the system, routing HTTP requests to either the Legacy Monolith (for not‑yet‑extracted functionality) or to newly created domain services (User, Product, Order, Payment, Review). Each service is a Python/Django application with its own schema in a shared PostgreSQL cluster, ensuring data ownership. Internal communication uses a hybrid model: synchronous HTTP for UI‑driven calls and asynchronous events via Amazon SNS/SQS for cross‑service workflows (e.g., order creation, payment processing). Services are deployed in ECS/Fargate with auto‑scaling groups across multiple AZs, backed by an RDS PostgreSQL instance and managed queues. Feature flags in the gateway enable gradual traffic shift during migration steps.
constraints_addressed: cost efficiency (use of managed services and auto‑scaling)
assumptions: Existing Django codebase can be refactored into separate apps.
Data can be partitioned per domain with minimal cross‑service joins.
Team has expertise in Python/Django and AWS managed services.
Compliance requirements are not yet defined; will be addressed when clarified.
open_risks: Data consistency during the dual‑write period of migration.
Operational overhead of managing multiple services and queues.
Potential latency introduced by asynchronous event processing.
Skill gap for operating event‑driven infrastructure on AWS.

migration_steps.title: Introduce API Gateway and routing layer
migration_steps.objective: Create a façade that abstracts the monolith and new services, enabling traffic routing via feature flags.
changes: Configure routes to Legacy Monolith for all existing endpoints
migration_steps.coexistence_or_data_strategy: All external traffic passes through the gateway; routing rules initially point to the monolith.
migration_steps.exit_condition: Gateway health checks pass and traffic is successfully routed.

migration_steps.title: Extract User Service
migration_steps.objective: Move user account management to an independent service.
changes: Migrate user tables to dedicated schema
Update API Gateway routes for /users to User Service
migration_steps.coexistence_or_data_strategy: Dual‑write during migration; feature flag gradually shifts traffic to User Service.
migration_steps.exit_condition: All user‑related API calls are served by User Service and tests pass.

migration_steps.title: Extract Product Service
changes: Migrate product tables to its schema
migration_steps.coexistence_or_data_strategy: Feature flag controls traffic split; data sync scripts keep legacy and new tables consistent.
migration_steps.exit_condition: Product API fully served by Product Service.

migration_steps.title: Extract Order Service with event-driven workflow
migration_steps.objective: Decouple order processing and enable asynchronous handling.
changes: Consume payment events for order state updates
migration_steps.coexistence_or_data_strategy: Orders created via gateway are persisted in both monolith and Order Service during cut‑over.
migration_steps.exit_condition: Order lifecycle managed entirely by Order Service.

migration_steps.title: Extract Payment Service
migration_steps.coexistence_or_data_strategy: Feature flag routes payment calls; events synchronize order status.
migration_steps.exit_condition: All payment interactions handled by Payment Service.

migration_steps.title: Extract Review Service
migration_steps.coexistence_or_data_strategy: Dual‑write and eventual consistency for existing reviews.
migration_steps.exit_condition: Review API fully served by Review Service.

migration_steps.title: Decommission Legacy Monolith
migration_steps.objective: Retire the original monolith after all capabilities are migrated.
changes: Remove monolith routes from API Gateway
migration_steps.coexistence_or_data_strategy: All traffic now handled by extracted services; data resides in service‑specific schemas.
migration_steps.exit_condition: No requests are routed to Legacy Monolith and monitoring confirms zero errors.

adrs.title: ADR-001: Service decomposition using Domain-Driven Design
adrs.context: The monolith tightly couples user, product, order, payment, and review capabilities, hindering independent scaling and evolution.
adrs.decision: Define bounded contexts aligned with business capabilities and implement each as an independent Django service.
adrs.rationale: DDD aligns service boundaries with natural domain divisions, reducing coupling and enabling independent deployment, which directly addresses scalability and maintainability goals.
negative_consequences: Need for data synchronization during migration

adrs.title: ADR-002: Service-specific data ownership
adrs.context: Shared database tables across domains cause tight coupling and hinder independent evolution.
adrs.decision: Each service owns its own schema within a shared PostgreSQL cluster; no service accesses another's tables directly.
adrs.rationale: Service‑owned data enforces boundaries, simplifies migrations, and supports independent scaling, matching the DDD approach.
alternatives_considered: Single shared schema for all services

adrs.title: ADR-003: Hybrid integration (sync UI, async events)
adrs.context: User‑facing interactions require low‑latency responses, while internal workflows benefit from decoupling.
adrs.decision: Use synchronous HTTP for UI‑driven calls via API Gateway and asynchronous event‑driven communication (SNS/SQS) for inter‑service processes.
adrs.rationale: Combines responsive user experience with scalable, fault‑tolerant backend processing, as recommended for e‑commerce workloads.
positive_consequences: Loose coupling and better fault isolation
negative_consequences: Added complexity of managing queues and eventual consistency

adrs.title: ADR-004: AWS auto-scaling and multi-AZ deployment
adrs.context: Peak traffic of up to 50,000 concurrent users requires elastic capacity and high availability.
adrs.decision: Deploy services in AWS ECS/Fargate with auto‑scaling groups and place them behind an Application Load Balancer across multiple Availability Zones. Use RDS Multi‑AZ for PostgreSQL.
adrs.rationale: AWS managed scaling and multi‑AZ provide the elasticity and resilience needed without manual capacity planning.
negative_consequences: Potential cost increase if scaling is not tuned

adrs.title: ADR-005: Incremental migration via Strangler Fig
adrs.context: The need to modernize without disrupting ongoing operations.
adrs.decision: Introduce a façade (API Gateway) and migrate capabilities one bounded context at a time, routing traffic via feature flags until the monolith can be retired.
adrs.rationale: Strangler Fig enables zero‑downtime migration, aligns with the incremental migration requirement, and leverages existing AWS routing capabilities.
negative_consequences: Complexity of dual‑write and routing logic

adrs.title: ADR-006: Preserve existing Python/Django and React stack
adrs.context: The repository already uses Python/Django for backend and React for frontend; no compelling requirement to replace them.
adrs.decision: Retain Python/Django for all new services and keep the React SPA unchanged, adding only AWS managed infrastructure where needed.
adrs.rationale: Reusing the existing stack minimizes rewrite effort, leverages team expertise, and reduces risk, while still achieving scalability via cloud services.
alternatives_considered: Rewrite services in a different language/framework
positive_consequences: Faster migration due to familiar codebase
negative_consequences: Potential limitations of Django for certain high‑throughput scenarios

components.name: Legacy Monolith
components.purpose: Existing Django monolith that currently implements all e‑commerce capabilities.
components.description: The current codebase provides user, product, order, payment, and review functionality. It will be gradually decomposed while remaining operational behind the API Gateway.
outputs: Domain events (during migration) via internal signals
security_considerations: Audit existing code for security vulnerabilities
scalability_considerations: Will be scaled via API Gateway routing until services replace it

components.name: API Gateway
components.purpose: Unified entry point for all client traffic, enabling routing, feature‑flag based traffic shifting, and security enforcement.
components.description: Deployed on AWS API Gateway (or an open‑source alternative) to forward requests to either the Legacy Monolith or the newly extracted services. Handles TLS termination and request authentication.
outputs: HTTP requests to Backend Services or Legacy Monolith
scalability_considerations: Built‑in auto‑scaling and regional redundancy

components.name: User Service
components.purpose: Manage user registration, authentication, profile data, and related events.
components.description: A Django application exposing REST endpoints for user CRUD, login, and profile updates. Owns the "user" schema in PostgreSQL and publishes UserCreated/Updated events.
inputs: UserCreated events from other services (if needed)
outputs: UserCreated / UserUpdated events to Message Queue
security_considerations: Store passwords with strong hashing (e.g., Argon2)
scalability_considerations: Stateless containers behind load balancer
Auto‑scaling based on request latency

components.name: Product Service
components.purpose: Provide product catalog management and search capabilities.
components.description: Handles product CRUD, image storage references, and search indexing. Owns the "product" schema.
scalability_considerations: Read replicas for high‑read traffic
Cache product data in Amazon ElastiCache

components.name: Order Service
components.purpose: Process customer orders, manage order lifecycle, and coordinate with payment and inventory.
components.description: Exposes order creation, status tracking, and order history APIs. Owns the "order" schema and participates in event‑driven workflows (OrderCreated, PaymentProcessed).
scalability_considerations: Stateless processing, auto‑scale based on order rate
Eventual consistency for payment updates

components.name: Payment Service
components.purpose: Integrate with external payment gateways and record transaction details.
components.description: Handles payment initiation, callback processing, and stores payment status. Owns the "payment" schema and emits PaymentProcessed events.
security_considerations: PCI‑DSS compliance: never store raw card data
Use HTTPS for all external calls
scalability_considerations: Horizontal scaling to handle bursty checkout traffic

components.name: Review Service
components.purpose: Collect, moderate, and display product reviews.
components.description: Provides endpoints for creating and retrieving reviews. Owns the "review" schema and publishes ReviewCreated events.
scalability_considerations: Cache recent reviews with Amazon ElastiCache

components.name: Frontend (React SPA)
components.purpose: Provide the customer‑facing web interface for browsing, shopping, and account management.
components.description: A React single‑page application consuming the API Gateway endpoints. Built with Redux for state management.
security_considerations: Use HTTPS for all API calls
scalability_considerations: Static assets served via CloudFront CDN
Client‑side rendering reduces backend load

components.name: PostgreSQL Cluster
components.purpose: Persist relational data for all domain services.
components.description: A managed Amazon RDS PostgreSQL instance with Multi‑AZ deployment. Each service uses its own schema, enforcing data ownership.
security_considerations: Encryption at rest and in transit
scalability_considerations: Automatic storage scaling
Read replicas for high read throughput

components.name: Message Queue (Amazon SQS)
components.purpose: Provide reliable asynchronous messaging between services.
components.description: Standard SQS queues used for event propagation (e.g., OrderCreated, PaymentProcessed). Supports at‑least‑once delivery and decouples producers from consumers.
scalability_considerations: Unlimited throughput, auto‑scales with load

components.name: Event Bus (Amazon SNS)
components.purpose: Broadcast domain events to multiple interested services.
components.description: SNS topics used for fan‑out of events such as OrderCreated, PaymentProcessed, and ReviewCreated, enabling multiple services to react.
outputs: Event notifications to subscribed SQS queues or Lambda functions
scalability_considerations: Highly scalable, supports millions of messages per second

judgment_reasons.repo_grounding: The repository contains a Django monolith with clearly separated apps (user, product, order, payment, review, address, core). The blueprint’s Strangler Fig decomposition extracts each of these apps into independent Django services, preserving the existing language and framework, which directly reflects the actual code structure.
judgment_reasons.flaw_detection: The blueprint and ADRs cover all functional requirements (user, product, order, payment, review) and non‑functional goals (50k concurrent users, high availability, incremental migration). The migration steps, auto‑scaling, multi‑AZ deployment, and API Gateway façade directly address the business goal of scalable, maintainable, zero‑downtime evolution.
judgment_reasons.adr_soundness: ADR‑004 (AWS auto‑scaling and multi‑AZ deployment) cites evidence ID KB‑E004, which the deterministic check flags as unrelated to its decision topic TOPIC‑4 (scaling and availability). The cited evidence pertains to integration style rather than scaling, breaking the soundness of the ADR.
judgment_reasons.best_practice_grounding: Because ADR‑004 cites unrelated evidence, the recommendation for auto‑scaling and multi‑AZ deployment is not properly grounded in retrieved knowledge. This violates best‑practice grounding, as the citation does not substantiate the decision.
judgment_reasons.refinement_readiness: The identified issues (evidence mismatch in ADR‑004) are specific and actionable, with clear corrective steps provided, enabling the architect to start a refinement pass without ambiguity.
